SINKRONIZED / ARIZONA FIELD ATLAS

Arizona is our home.What happens beneath it matters.

Our cities, farms and desert communities depend on groundwater that lies out of sight. When water levels decline, the land above can slowly sink.

Sinkronized puts NASA’s new NISAR radar satellite to work on Arizona: we test its first year of data against a decade of older satellite records and published groundwater research, so the evidence is easier to explore—and its limits easier to understand.

WHY WE BUILT THIS

A familiar landscape. An overlooked change.

Arizona is where we live, learn and imagine our future. Understanding what is happening below the surface matters just as much as understanding what we can see above it.

01 / THE PLACE

A landscape we share

From expanding cities to agricultural valleys, our communities depend on groundwater. Much of that dependence is invisible in everyday life.

02 / THE CHANGE

Movement we rarely notice

In Arizona's alluvial basins, groundwater withdrawal can compact sediments, lower the ground surface and contribute to earth fissures. USGS research documents these changes.

03 / OUR RESPONSE

Make the evidence accessible

We built Sinkronized to connect radar measurements, observation dates and uncertainty with groundwater research—helping people ask more informed questions without pretending every pixel has a known cause.

The distinction matters: agriculture is a major estimated water-use sector in the Willcox Basin, and a 2023 peer-reviewed study links agricultural expansion with groundwater decline. That supports regional context, not attributing an individual satellite observation to a particular farm, well or development.

WHY THIS MATTERS

A clearer view of the ground we share.

Making the evidence understandable helps people see where closer investigation, monitoring and better-informed decisions may be needed.

01 / COMMUNITIES

Understand your surroundings

Residents and students can see which places have been studied, what movement the satellites detected and where measurements are incomplete.

02 / PLANNING & WATER

See patterns worth investigating

Planners, engineers and water managers can put ground-motion evidence alongside longer-term context when thinking about infrastructure and groundwater management.

03 / RESEARCH & CONSERVATION

Ask more precise questions

Researchers and conservation groups can explore measured trends and uncertainty while recognizing that radar cannot establish causes or directly measure habitat impacts.

RESEARCH / HISTORICAL CONTEXT

What the research already tells us

These findings are from published scientific research and agency records. They provide historical context, not measurements made by the Sinkronized processing pipeline.

01 / THE MECHANISM Groundwater loss

Pumping can compact aquifers permanently.

When groundwater levels fall, compressible sediments can compact, lowering the land surface and permanently reducing water-storage capacity.

USGS · Subsidence science ↗
02 / ELOY, ARIZONA 1.09 m

Measured historical ground lowering.

USGS documented 1.09 metres of subsidence caused by groundwater withdrawal at a monitoring site near Eloy between 1965 and 1983.

USGS · Epstein (1987) ↗
03 / WILLCOX, ARIZONA 155,805 acre-feet

Estimated agricultural water use in 2022.

ADWR identifies agriculture as Willcox's largest water-use sector. Research also associates expanded agricultural land with falling groundwater levels.

ADWR · Willcox groundwater conditions ↗ Geosciences · 2023 research paper ↗

Supported: groundwater extraction is a documented driver of land subsidence, and agriculture is a significant pumping pressure in these basins. Not supported by this map alone: attributing a specific new satellite observation to an individual farm, well or facility.

WHAT WE ARE STUDYING

Not just whether the land moves. How confidently we can say so.

We investigate ground movement in the study areas supplied by our team’s current dataset. Satellite radar reveals changes along its viewing direction; real acquisition dates, stable reference areas, data quality and comparisons with Arizona Department of Water Resources research help us interpret those signals.

We distinguish the longer Sentinel-1 record from newer, preliminary NISAR measurements. Where the evidence is weak or missing, the website says so instead of presenting a guess as a result.

Why look in both directions? +
01 / ASCENDING South to north ↗

The satellite generally travels northward while observing the surface at a slanted angle.

02 / DESCENDING North to south ↘

The satellite generally travels southward and observes from a different slanted perspective.

Together, these views can strengthen confidence and help separate some motion components. One direction alone cannot establish a unique vertical sinking rate.

01 / LOCATE

Choose a study area drawn from the team’s latest dataset—not a fixed list.

02 / READ

Inspect measured movement, acquisition dates and comparisons where records exist.

03 / QUESTION

Check confidence, viewing direction and missing observations before drawing conclusions.

NASA NISAR / FIRST YEAR, TESTED

NASA’s newest radar satellite, tested on Arizona.

NISAR has revisited Arizona about every 12 days since late October 2025 (a few visits were skipped). We asked one plain question: does its first year see the same sinking that ten years of older satellite data show? These results are our own processing of NASA’s Provisional data.

01 / SAME PLACES match

NISAR finds the same sinking basin.

How we know

Across map blocks at Willcox, NISAR’s one-year pattern lines up with the ten-year Sentinel-1 pattern (correlation ; 1 is a perfect match, 0 is none). Where one satellite sees sinking, so does the other.

02 / A CLEANER SIGNAL −% noise

NISAR’s weather correction works.

How we know

NISAR provides tables of how moist air delays the radar signal but leaves them for users to apply. We tested applying them both ways and kept the direction that helps: it cut the scatter in our Willcox series from to mm. The wrong direction made it much worse.

03 / NOT YET A SPEED to confirm

One year is still too short for a speed.

How we know

Noise in single observation dates dominates a short record. At Willcox’s cm/yr we estimate NISAR needs about years of unbroken data for a 90% chance of a confirmed rate. Today that chance is about %. At Eloy ( cm/yr, started June 2026) it is about .

Where NISAR and Sentinel-1 do not agree

Over the six months both watched (Oct 2025–Apr 2026) their changes did not match (correlation ): about 1 cm of movement in six months is smaller than the noise. In the sinking areas NISAR also reads faster than Sentinel-1 ( against cm/yr, relative to the surroundings); we cannot yet tell whether that is noise or a recent speed-up. Over its full year NISAR’s playa change was cm, close to Sentinel-1’s long-term trend of cm/yr, but one date carries 1–1.5 cm of error, so this is consistent, not proven.

From the other side

NISAR’s ascending track looks at Willcox from the opposite direction. Over the same June to October months ( days), the areas Sentinel-1 shows sinking changed by mm in the ascending data (95% range to ) and mm in the descending data ( to ), relative to the rest, against mm expected from Sentinel-1’s long-term rate. Negative means moving away from the satellite. The difference between the two directions would reveal sideways motion; it is mm ( to ), too uncertain to say anything. Over so short a span the two directions’ whole-map patterns are mostly noise, so we do not compare them block by block.

NISAR BACKSCATTER / WHAT IS ON TOP

Radar also shows what covers the ground: farmland and desert.

How strongly the ground reflects the signal depends on what is on it. We read NISAR’s reflected signal in two channels (HH and HV) on dates, and compared irrigated cropland, taken from USDA’s 2025 Cropland Data Layer, with desert shrubland.

01 / WHERE THE CROPS ARE % of the sinking area

Farmland is a small part of the land but a large part of the sinking.

How we know

Cropland covers % of the Willcox study box but % of the area Sentinel-1 shows sinking ( times its share), about acres of crops.

02 / WHAT THE RADAR READS − cm/yr, may be inflated

Cropland reads as sinking faster than nearby desert.

How we know

On Sentinel-1’s ten-year record, cropland cells read cm/yr lower than desert cells (95% range to ). % of cropland cells read faster than 1 cm/yr of sinking, against % of desert cells. Farmland can inflate this kind of reading (see below), and it shows where, not why.

03 / HOW NISAR TELLS THEM APART score

NISAR sees farming as change through the year, not as brightness.

How we know

On dry dates, how much the HH signal swings over the year separates cropland from desert with a score of (0.5 is a coin flip, 1 is perfect). Average HH brightness scores : no help. The HV swing scores .

Farmland can fool this radar

Published studies find that changing soil moisture and crops add apparent sinking to Sentinel-1-type (C-band) radar over fields: a systematic bias of up to several millimetres a year in general, and an estimated 2–4 cm a year for cotton in California, with the largest gaps against L-band in orchards such as pistachios, which also grow at Willcox. So part of the gap above may not be real sinking. What points the same way independently: NISAR’s L-band, less affected by this, also puts cropland lower (see below), and Willcox farmland has long been studied as a subsidence area.

Other cautions

Rain brightens every land type at once: NISAR’s scene-wide brightness follows the previous three days’ rainfall (rank correlation for HH, for HV; rainfall from the ERA5 weather reanalysis on a 25 km grid). So we compare crops with desert on the same date and re-checked the scores using only the dry dates. Not settled: NISAR’s own L-band rates also put cropland below desert ( cm/yr), but only cropland cells stay coherent all year, so we do not trust that size. The land-cover map describes the 2025 growing season while the radar year runs to November 2026, and fields rotate. None of this shows which farm, well or user caused any sinking.

PUMPING / WHERE THE WATER IS TAKEN

Where farms are estimated to pump the most, the ground sinks the most.

The USGS maps every irrigated field in the Willcox basin and estimates how much groundwater each one drew in 2024. We laid those estimates over the ten-year Sentinel-1 sinking map. The pumping figures are a model’s estimates, not meter readings.

01 / THE PUMPING acre-feet a year

About acre-feet from irrigated acres.

How we know

USGS counts irrigated fields, all watered from groundwater, in 2024. An acre-foot is the water that covers an acre one foot deep.

02 / WHERE IT SINKS cm/yr where pumping is highest

Sinking steps up with the pumping nearby.

How we know

Sorting the basin into 300 m blocks by the estimated pumping within km, the typical block reads cm/yr with no field nearby, with a little pumping, with more, and with the most (negative means sinking).

03 / HOW STRONG correlation

A clear link, but mostly about where the fields are.

How we know

Ranking blocks by pumping and by sinking gives (95% range to ); inside the pumped area alone. Irrigated acreage by itself scores , so the modelled volumes add little beyond where the irrigated land is (, range to ).

What this does not show

Matching places is not proof of cause: the pumping is a 2024 model estimate while the radar rate averages ten years, and C-band radar can over-read sinking over farmland (see above). The field-by-field test is inconclusive: only % of fields kept a usable 30 m radar reading, mostly idle land, orchards and vineyards, while almost all of the field-crop fields (small grains, cover crops, alfalfa, corn and cotton) lost it ( kept), so the heaviest pumpers are missing. Across the pumped fields that did keep one, pumping per acre and sinking were barely related (, range to ). Water levels in wells, geology and the depth of the clay layers are not included.
